title: After 1997 south-east Australian streams drained 25-38% faster at equal flow than in any era since 1911, unlike after the WWII drought, and returned to the 1957-1996 rate by 2020-2025 (29+114 gauges)
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff fell 12-25% below its 1951-1996 rain relation and stayed low; long records also show high runoff at equal rain before 1957. Is the post-1997 deficit a drought-induced state shift or part of a multidecadal process? Rain-based tests depend on the rain product, so we used a rain-free indicator: the stream recession rate at equal flow and month (drainage index R, log units, reference 1957-1996). Approach: quantization-robust recession segments (runs of 7+ non-increasing days) in 29 SE-AU and 7 Queensland BoM records from before 1946 to 2025, and 114 SE-AU and 33 Queensland CAMELS-AUS catchments (1951-2021); 2x2-degree cell bootstrap; plan written before any recession result, with two addenda (estimator change, data QC, post hoc list). Results: R was +0.32 (95% CI +0.16 to +0.45) in 1997-2009 and +0.22 (+0.12 to +0.30) in 2010-2021, above every era of 1911-1996 (largest +0.04); broad set +0.30 and +0.22. The WWII drought did not speed drainage (-0.03; Millennium minus WWII drought +0.34, +0.21 to +0.42, with a smaller rain deficit). R follows multi-year wetness, but with wetness removed the post-1997 excess stayed (+0.18, +0.16). In the high-runoff 1946-1956 era R was -0.26 (-0.40 to -0.17). Block R and block efficiency correlated at -0.67 (-0.84 to +0.14), and faster-draining catchments lost more runoff after 2010 (Spearman -0.41) and more rain sensitivity (-0.32). The 1959-1971 and 1983-1995 lows had R of +0.00 and +0.06. In 2020-2025 R was -0.01 (-0.05 to +0.06). Queensland had the same drainage history but runoff at equal rain was +48% after 2010. Conclusion: the post-1997 drainage change was not a generic drought response and not permanent; drainage and efficiency moved together in opposite directions over the century, which supports one multidecadal storage-drainage process. Faster drainage alone does not make the loss; its cause remains open. Limitations: few long gauges (8 in Victoria), coarse early stage resolution (the pre-1957 drainage result is not robust to it), rating shape not tested, linear wetness and efficiency models, several post hoc analyses, 2020-2025 efficiency unresolved.

citations.reason: It found faster recessions after 1997 in CAMELS-AUS; we extend the recession test to 1911-2025 with a quantization-robust estimator and confirm it to 2021.
We use its annual rain model form and its finding of a rain-sensitivity loss after 1997.
Its earlier lows were parallel shifts; we find they also had almost no drainage signature.
It found that runoff stayed high after the WWII drought; we find that drainage did not speed up after it either.
Context: climate explains little of the multidecadal efficiency change; we add a rain-free drainage indicator.
Context: the 1946-1956 surplus is not explained by monthly climate; we find slow drainage in the same era.
Context: the early surplus is not a land-clearing effect and may involve flow measurement; we test stage-resolution and rating-scale artefacts in recessions.
Context: timing of the Victorian step and the NSW decline.
Context: the 1997 step followed the winter-rain share.
Context: rain-product choice changes runoff-change estimates; this motivates a rain-free indicator.
Context: fixed rain-gauge networks confirm the post-1997 deficit.
Context: Victorian catchments stayed in a low-runoff state to 2025; our drainage index returned to the reference in 2020-2025.
Context: climate terms fitted before 1997 explain little of the deficit.
Context: rain intensity, seasonality, PET and the IPO do not explain century-scale efficiency.
